CHAIR ( Senator Cox ): I declare open this hearing of the Community Affairs Legislation Committee into the 2025-26 additional estimates. I begin by acknowledging the traditional custodians of the land on which we meet today. I pay my respects to their elders past and present and extend that respect to Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples here today. The committee has fixed Thursday 9 April 2026 as the date of return for answers to questions taken on notice. The committee would appreciate if senators could please provide any written questions on notice to the secretariat by Thursday 19 February 2026. The committee's proceedings today will begin with the Department of Health, Disability and Ageing under outcome 2, Individual health benefits.

Under standing order 26, the committee must take all evidence in public session. This includes answers to questions on notice. I remind all witnesses that, in giving evidence to the committee, they are protected by parliamentary privilege. It is unlawful for anyone to threaten or disadvantage a witness on account of evidence given to a committee. Such action may be treated by the Senate as a contempt. It is also a contempt to give false or misleading evidence.

The Senate has endorsed the following test of relevance of questions at estimates hearings: any questions going to the operations or financial positions of the departments and agencies which are seeking funds in estimates are relevant questions for the purpose of estimates hearings. I remind all officers the Senate has resolved that there are no areas in connection with the expenditure of public funds where any person has the discretion to withhold details or explanations from the parliament or its committees unless the parliament has expressly provided otherwise.

The Senate has also resolved that an officer of a department of the Commonwealth shall not be asked to give opinions on matters of policy and shall be given reasonable opportunity to refer questions asked of the officer to superior officers or to a minister. This resolution does not preclude questions asking for explanations of policies, or factual questions about when and how policies were adopted. Witnesses are reminded of the Senate's order specifying the process by which a claim of public interest immunity should be raised. I incorporate the public interest immunity statement into the Hansard.

The extract reads as follows —

Public interest immunity claims

That the Senate—

(a) notes that ministers and officers have continued to refuse to provide information to Senate committees without properly raising claims of public interest immunity as required by past resolutions of the Senate;

(b) reaffirms the principles of past resolutions of the Senate by this order, to provide ministers and officers with guidance as to the proper process for raising public interest immunity claims and to consolidate those past resolutions of the Senate;

(c) orders that the following operate as an order of continuing effect:

(1) If:

(a) a Senate committee, or a senator in the course of proceedings of a committee, requests information or a document from a Commonwealth department or agency; and

(b) an officer of the department or agency to whom the request is directed believes that it may not be in the public interest to disclose the information or document to the committee, the officer shall state to the committee the ground on which the officer believes that it may not be in the public interest to disclose the information or document to the committee, and specify the harm to the public interest that could result from the disclosure of the information or document.

(2) If, after receiving the officer's statement under paragraph (1), the committee or the senator requests the officer to refer the question of the disclosure of the information or document to a responsible minister, the officer shall refer that question to the minister.

(3) If a minister, on a reference by an officer under paragraph (2), concludes that it would not be in the public interest to disclose the information or document to the committee, the minister shall provide to the committee a statement of the ground for that conclusion, specifying the harm to the public interest that could result from the disclosure of the information or document.

(4) A minister, in a statement under paragraph (3), shall indicate whether the harm to the public interest that could result from the disclosure of the information or document to the committee could result only from the publication of the information or document by the committee, or could result, equally or in part, from the disclosure of the information or document to the committee as in camera evidence.

(5) If, after considering a statement by a minister provided under paragraph (3), the committee concludes that the statement does not sufficiently justify the withholding of the information or document from the committee, the committee shall report the matter to the Senate.

(6) A decision by a committee not to report a matter to the Senate under paragraph (5) does not prevent a senator from raising the matter in the Senate in accordance with other procedures of the Senate.

(7) A statement that information or a document is not published, or is confidential, or consists of advice to, or internal deliberations of, government, in the absence of specification of the harm to the public interest that could result from the disclosure of the information or document, is not a statement that meets the requirements of paragraph (1) or (4).

(8) If a minister concludes that a statement under paragraph (3) should more appropriately be made by the head of an agency, by reason of the independence of that agency from ministerial direction or control, the minister shall inform the committee of that conclusion and the reason for that conclusion, and shall refer the matter to the head of the agency, who shall then be required to provide a statement in accordance with paragraph (3).

(d) requires the Procedure Committee to review the operation of this order and report to the Senate by 20 August 2009.

(13 May 2009 J.1941)

CHAIR: It gives me great pleasure to now welcome Senator the Hon. Jenny McAllister, Minister for the National Disability Insurance Scheme, representing the Minister for Health, Disability and Ageing. Minister, do you wish to make an opening statement?

Senator McAllister: No, thank you.

CHAIR: I also welcome back the Secretary of the Department of Health, Disability and Ageing, Mr Blair Comley PSM. Mr Comley, do you wish to make an opening statement?

Mr Comley : No, thank you.

Senator McAllister: I should have indicated earlier in the last hearing that I would hope to make a brief opening statement about the NDIS, but it seems more sensible to do that at that point in the program.

CHAIR: Yes, that would be great. I now call officers from the Department of Health, Disability and Ageing in relation to outcome 2, Individual health benefits. Senator Ruston, you have the call.

Senator RUSTON: Could I ask some questions about the bulk-billing targets. I am really starting to wonder whether we're having groundhog day, because I'm going to ask you exactly the same questions that I asked you at the last three estimates in relation to the announcement of additional funding put into expanding the bulk-billing initiative in Australia when the government said they were anticipating that they would have a bulk-billing rate of 90 per cent by the end of the decade. I asked you at the last two estimates if you were in a position to provide me with—I don't mind what you call them: the targets, the estimates or whatever the word is that you want to use; let's not be tricky about words—the model or the target trajectory of the increase in the bulk-billing rate from when the initiative started to when it's anticipated to be at 90 per cent by 2030. Do you have those year-on-year numbers?

Ms Shakespeare : Some of the information about the annual estimates was provided at our hearings on 4 December. That's at page four of the Hansard record for the hearings, and we can provide that to you. That had the yearly breakdown for the estimates for both the bulk-billing incentive program and the bulk-billing incentives under the Medicare Benefits Schedule. We provided further information in response to your questions on notice. The most relevant one is Senate estimates question on notice 3163 from 2025. I could take you through some information that was contained in there as well.

Senator RUSTON: All I'm looking for is a document that shows the bulk-billing rate on the start date of the initiative, in November 2025, and on whatever date you've got in 2030 when you believe you'll get to 90 per cent. What is the trajectory? Do you have that?

Ms Shakespeare : We have a target for the bulk-billing rate by 2030 of 90 per cent. No previous targets have been set by any government on an annual basis or other basis for the Medicare bulk-billing rate. This is the first time a government has set a target for bulk-billing.

Senator RUSTON: Sure. I understand that, and it has been announced and commented on a lot of times. I totally accept 90 per cent by 2030. We had 77.7 per cent or whatever it was when this initiative commenced. It said, 'This initiative is estimating that we will be at 90 per cent by 2030.' None of us are disagreeing with that. I just want to know what the line is. Does it go up and then plateau off? Does it go in a straight line? Are you expecting all of it to happen in the last two minutes? How did you get to 90 per cent in 2030? What were the assumptions along the way that said, 'This is going to increase'? Quite frankly, all I want is the modelling to show the trajectory to get to 90 per cent by 2030. That's all I want.

Ms Shakespeare : As set out in that Senate estimates question on notice response 3163, in preparing the impact analysis for this measure, which set out our assumptions and informed government decisions about whether or not to implement these measures, the department estimated these initiatives will cause the GP bulk-billing rates to increase by 10.5 percentage points by 2028-29. That's set out in more detail at pages 39 and 56 of the published impact analysis. This included an estimated 4.5 percentage point increase to bulk-billing rates due to the expansion of eligibility for bulk-billing incentive items. This is underpinned by an assumption that the bulk-billing rate for patients who were currently ineligible for a bulk-billing incentive would increase by 10 percentage points. This assumption was based on the observed difference in bulk-billing rates between concessional and non-concessional patients who were eligible for bulk-billing incentives due to their age and further adjusted to account for trends in bulk-billing by patient age.

The department estimated that the Bulk Billing Practice Incentive Program would lead to a further six percentage point increase to the GP bulk-billing rate by 2028-29. This impact is dependent on the expansion of the bulk-billing incentives as those bulk-billing incentives that we discussed earlier reduce the earnings gap between bulk-billed and privately billed services. The department estimated that around 4,800 general practices would be financially better off if they joined the Bulk Billing Practice Incentive Program and bulk-billed all GP non-referred attendant services for Medicare-eligible patients. The department used Medicare claims data to build an income model for each of the 6,600 general practices registered with the practice incentive program. The model considered each GP provider's and practice's revenue from MBS benefits, bulk-billing incentives and patient fees. We've got a quite detailed explanation of the assumptions. It does not include a trajectory for bulk-billing rates. Our modelling and assumptions were on different factors.

Senator RUSTON: In terms of the bulk-billing rates and the number of fully bulk-billed practices, because they're the two metrics that we've got here, you had no number for either the bulk-billing rate or the number of practices that were likely to join up today?

Ms Shakespeare : No. We have annual numbers in the impact analysis for the number of practices we expected on an annual basis to join the program. That is set out at page 61 of the impact analysis that I said has been published.

Senator RUSTON: So you don't have a target of what you're expecting today?

Ms Shakespeare : I'm sorry? A target of—

Senator RUSTON: You couldn't actually go in at any point in time and say, 'We are expecting that this will be the target at this particular time'? They're just the annual targets for one thing, no annual targets for bulk-billing?

Ms Shakespeare : We had annual estimates of numbers of practices that would join the Bulk Billing Practice Incentive Program. They have been published. We are currently exceeding those published estimates.

Senator RUSTON: Did you model the incentive program?

Ms Shakespeare : Yes.

Senator RUSTON: Is that available?

Ms Shakespeare : That's explained at the question on notice response 3163 and also in great detail in the impact analysis.

Senator RUSTON: It seems very interesting that we don't seem to be able to get any granular detail about this, but the minister is out there quoting that we are well ahead of wherever we were expecting to be.

Ms Shakespeare : As I said, we have numbers of practices that were expected on an annual basis to join up to the practice incentive program. Those are published at page 61 of the impact analysis. The target—it was not a target, I should say. The estimate for 2025-26 in terms of number of practices joined was 1,603. We know that the number of practices that have registered so far is in excess of that number.

Senator RUSTON: Okay. We'll keep trying to get the information, but it seems like it's not very easy to get. In that impact analysis, the bulk-billing rate target metric, whatever you want to call it, was 87.8 per cent by 2028-29. That's the 10 per cent increase that you were talking about?

Mr McCabe : Yes, that's correct.

Senator RUSTON: And 3,600 GP practices would become fully bulk-billed clinics by 2028?

Mr Roddam : Yes, 3,600 practices are expected to sign up by 2027-28.

Senator RUSTON: And 4,800 by 2029-30?

Mr Roddam : By 2028-29.

Senator RUSTON: 2028-29?

Mr Roddam : Yes.

Senator RUSTON: Is that where it maxes out, or have you got further data past that point?

Mr Roddam : No further data past that point.

Senator RUSTON: So the bulk-billing rate goes to 2030, but the practice incentive only goes to 2029?

Mr Roddam : The estimates of take up.

Senator RUSTON: It also projects a 50 per cent decrease in total out-of-pocket costs for GP non-referred; is that correct?

Mr McCabe : Yes, that's what the policy impact statement said.

Senator RUSTON: Are these formal targets once you've got out to that?

Mr Comley : There are no formal targets other than the 2030 target of 90 per cent. All the other things we're talking about are estimates that underpin what we anticipate happening based on the modelling, but they are not targets.

Senator RUSTON: The question is: what is the government going to be measured against in relation to this particular initiative before that time? I accept we can't be measuring anything yet and that we need time. I'm not being critical. Clearly, there has been an uptick, and this is all good, because we want Australians to be able to get access to more affordable health care, so I have no criticism on that front. I'm just trying to understand how we measure in the middle of next year, as an example, the success or otherwise of this measure. It's $8.5 billion of taxpayers' money, and I can't find any measure which the government is prepared to stand by in terms of the success or failure of this initiative. What was expected in terms of success? You can't have a success measure in 2030, because there's nothing to measure against on the way through. What are the metrics by which you are expecting to measure the success or otherwise of this program before you get to these more formally announced numbers for 2028?

Ms Shakespeare : As set out in the impact analysis, it does require the department to include information about how measures would be evaluated, and we've explained how we would establish evaluation plans as the measure is implemented. I think the next key decision point, as set out in that impact analysis, in terms of having the evaluation plan worked up and then put into place, is 2027.

Senator RUSTON: When will we see the metrics that that evaluation plan will be measuring it against?

Ms Shakespeare : The department is working on that at the moment, and there will be metrics that we need to develop at a national level. We also need to make sure that we are able to evaluate how the measure is impacting particular communities and regions. This is a complex evaluation, and we need to develop it properly. We've set out information about how we plan to do that and the timeframes for developing the evaluation plan in the impact analysis that has been published.

Senator RUSTON: Can you just walk me through this. You're starting the process to develop an evaluation plan, so when do you expect to have that evaluation plan finalised, in terms of understanding the metrics of your evaluation process?

Ms Shakespeare : As set out in the impact analysis, the key decision point for the evaluation plan metrics is later this year and then implementation from the following year.

Senator RUSTON: When do you expect to have that reported back? You're working through it this year, to design the framework in which you're going to measure. You're going to implement that plan in 2027. When do you anticipate that you will have the findings of that evaluation?

Ms Shakespeare : I do think that depends on the extent of the metrics in there, how we're going to collect the information, how we're going to conduct the evaluation, whether it's within the department or whether we get independent involvement. I'm not sure at this stage, but we can certainly provide you, on notice, the information about the evaluation plan that was included in the impact analysis. That's also published, and it's available for anybody to see. We'll keep you updated. We're certainly very closely monitoring all of the data. We have MBS data published on a regular basis. There is a lot of interest in these measures, so we will be continuing to make information available about how it's tracking, ahead of the formal evaluation.

Senator McAllister: Can I say that, of course, there is substantial interest in Medicare because it is a prized and much loved Australian institution. I was pleased to hear you indicate that the coalition now supports an increase in bulk-billing. Your previous proposition, as I understood it, was that bulk-billing was unsustainable. In terms of the published data that came out—

Senator RUSTON: Where did you get that piece of information—that the coalition's position with bulk-billing was unsustainable?

Senator McAllister: I think it was your public comments about the public health system being unsustainable. You're sure welcome to clarify those at any time.

Senator RUSTON: If you're going to verbal me, you need to verbal me directly.

Senator McAllister: In terms of—

CHAIR: Senator Ruston—

Senator RUSTON: I'm finding it quite offensive that I'm being verballed. The minister is actually saying something that I've never said.

CHAIR: Okay. You can—

Senator McAllister: I've seen you put it so many times—saying that it's unsustainable. Anyway, if you say that that is not your position, that's terrific and I accept that.

CHAIR: Sorry, Minister. I'm okay for you to ask for that—to challenge that even—but while the minister is providing her statement, if we don't interrupt and go back and forth in that, that would be helpful. You will get the call back once the minister has finished speaking. I give the call to you, Minister.

Senator McAllister: The recently published data is obviously very encouraging. As the officials have indicated, the estimates of where we expected to be, in terms of practices, is set out in the impact analysis. We expected to be at around 3,600 practices in 2028. It's three months in and we're quite close to that. That is a positive outcome for Australians. They were facing a situation where bulk-billing was in freefall at the end of the Liberal government period. We are now seeing a turnaround. I think Australians will think that that is a very good outcome.

Senator RUSTON: Just to reiterate what I said—and I will reiterate this again a million times—the coalition absolutely supports Australians getting access to timely and affordable primary health care. That has never changed and will never change. I'm just keen to go back. All I'm trying to determine here is how you, as a government, intend to measure the success or failure of this $8.5 billion initiative. Could you guarantee to me that the analysis that Ms Shakespeare outlined earlier in her contribution will be completed, published and available to the Australian public prior to the next election?

Senator McAllister: I think the officials have set out the work that they intend to do. I don't have anything further to add to the timeline set out by Ms Shakespeare.

Senator RUSTON: Can I just make it very, very clear here: you are not prepared to put on the record today that you're not prepared to guarantee that you will allow the public to see the measure of success or failure of an $8.5 billion initiative of your government, prior to going to the next round of polls.

Senator McAllister: Just yesterday, the minister put out a press release explaining the progress that has been made. I think you will see our government very regularly communicating about the progress that is being made under this initiative.

Senator RUSTON: I take that as a no.

Senator McAllister: You should not take it in that way at all. I can't be clearer. The minister speaks about this regularly. Data is in the public domain. Our approach for 2030 is very clear. The expectations about the policy initiatives we've adopted are in the impact analysis. Work is ongoing to deepen the way that we will evaluate the impact of this policy. This is a policy we're very proud of. Because Australians value Medicare and Labor built Medicare, it's our intention to strengthen it. You will continue to see this be a focus for this government.

Senator ROBERTS: At the December 2025 Senate estimates, Associate Professor Dr Dio, you indicated that lawyers prepare their reports from the review scheme but that the committee members review the reports. In what way does the PSR monitor the performance of the committee—including if the committee has read the entire report and the material presented to it before signing it off?

Prof. Di Dio : The committee diligently reads the draft reports and the final reports, and we have staff who liaise with the committee at various stages after draft reports and final reports have been sent to them. So should for any reason a committee member not do their duty and read in the draft report, the legal officer in charge of giving service to that committee would firstly of course remind the committee members to review the report, and if they do not, they would then come to me. But that's a theoretical possibility, because I cannot recall that happening.

Senator ROBERTS: The PSR committee process is supposed to be a peer review process performed by doctors. Why then don't the doctors write their own reports? If administrative support is needed, why are lawyers drafting their reports instead of administrative or secretarial staff, which would come at a lower cost to the department?

Prof. Di Dio : Because the reports are incredibly important. We are passionate about according natural justice and procedural fairness to all practitioners under review. It is my view that the best way to do that is to have the best qualified, quality people writing those reports. Reports of this nature would be best written by people who are very good at supporting doctors in providing their reports.

Senator ROBERTS: 'Best qualified' to me would seem to be the doctors—and then trimmed up or modified by the lawyers.

Ms Weichert : The lawyers are writing up what the doctors have formed a view about as part of that committee process, as part of the hearing process, the concerns they have put to a person under review and the things that have come back—the lawyers are just putting it together. They are the doctors' concerns or the medical practitioners' concerns. It is they who sign off on the report, who approve the report. They are the peer review committee members' views.

Senator ROBERTS: If it can be shown that a lawyer spends over 150 hours drafting a report, but a committee member only spends seven to 10 hours reviewing the material and reading the report, is this truly considered by the PSR to be a legitimate peer review?

Ms Weichert : That's not taking into account any of the time that was spent in the hearing, in questioning and the time that the committee members have turned the matter throughout the process.

Prof. Di Dio : A hearing might take eight days; it might take 50 or 60 hours. The prehearing reading might take many, many hours. The contemplation of what happened during the committee hearing might take the committee members many, many hours to turn their mind to it.

Senator ROBERTS: Over the past three years, as an average, what percentage of the total services reviewed has the committee found the services provided by doctors to be inappropriate?

Prof. Di Dio : I will have to take that on notice.

Senator ROBERTS: This question is about general practitioners. The Royal Australian College of General Practitioners recognises 37 specific interest groups as subspecialities. If a GP is under review by the committee, is it correct that there is no legal requirement for the committee members to share the same subspecialty? For example, if a GP practices solely in aerospace medicine, there's no legal requirement for the committee to have any experience in aerospace medicine, because they all fall within the category of general practitioners. Why is there no subspeciality matching?

Prof. Di Dio : The subspecialty matching is that members of the committee are general practitioners. But the PSR strives to find general practitioners who have experience in those matters. I can assure you that for some practitioners who are in craft groups that are exotic, as you say, like me—I have particular special interests—we try to match those as much as we can. But, under the law, a general practitioner can review a fellow general practitioner.

Senator ROBERTS: Is it correct that the legislation allows just three committee members to decide what is unacceptable to the general body of general practitioners? In deciding what the general body of general practitioners find unacceptable, do the committee members have to have any regard to any external resources or consideration of other doctors? Do the lawyers draft that part of the report as well, about what the general body of doctors think?

Prof. Di Dio : One of the things that we train committee members to do, to absolutely and scrupulously give fairness to the practitioners under review, is try as much as possible to ask one question at a time to avoid the risk of the practitioner missing the opportunity to respond to any and all of the questions put to them. I'd be very grateful if you could ask me the first couple, and I'll go through them with you systematically.

Senator ROBERTS: Is it correct that the legislation allows just three committee members to decide what is unacceptable to the general body of practitioners?

Prof. Di Dio : Yes.

Ms Weichert : It's at least three. There are certain circumstances where there could be additional committee members appointed, but it is usually three.

Senator ROBERTS: In deciding what the general body of general practitioners find unacceptable, do the committee members have to have any regard to any external resources or consideration of other doctors?

Prof. Di Dio : The committee members have to have regard to all of the evidence before them so that they can—

Senator ROBERTS: All of the evidence before them?

Prof. Di Dio : Yes. The committee members welcome from the practitioner any materials that they wish to submit as further evidence either before, during or after the hearing.

Senator ROBERTS: While PSR committees are intended to operate as expert peer-review bodies, concerns include the absence of a presiding judge, the lack of merits review, the inability to cross-examine the committee on what they believe to be the views of the general bodies, the downweighting of significant evidence, limited engagement with defence submissions and a lack of transparency. Why do PSR procedures deny these basic elements of procedural fairness and justice, and how does the PSR contend that the peer-review function is being properly exercised in their absence?

Prof. Di Dio : Could you ask the six points one at a time, and I'll gladly respond to them.

Senator ROBERTS: They're intended to operate as expert peer review bodies. Concerns include the absence of a presiding judge.

Prof. Di Dio : The process is a peer-review process. So, if somebody is trying to find out whether I've engaged in inappropriate practice, then the best placed people to do that are my peers, not a judge.

Ms Weichert : And, ultimately, we are applying the scheme as it is set out in the Health Insurance Act, so that provides for a committee—

Senator ROBERTS: That may be the problem. The lack of merits review?

Senator RUSTON: Not as a hypothetical but just as an example, is it correct that services could potentially be offered through a school system in one state and through a different community service mechanism in another state? Senator RUSTON: No worries. In terms of the development of this, I'm interested in what measures are in place to ensure that the states and territories actually do adhere to the fundamental principles outlined in the Thriving Kids agreement.

Senator HANSON: Just about Thriving Kids: my understanding is it's basically identical to the program for childhood intervention services that is now provided in the NDIS. Is that correct?

This reform will move away from a pure therapy based model to one that focuses on—sure, there might be a little bit of therapy that is evidence based and needed for the child to achieve milestones, but there's a much greater focus on supporting families in community where they're already interacting with other services and building the capacity of the family and the child through those existing mechanisms.

Senator HANSON: Is Thriving Kids looking at doing it in the educational system? Senator HANSON: But doesn't that happen now with the NDIS? I know parents who have the services available to them under NDIS. This is going to be another department, isn't it? This is going to cost taxpayers billions of dollars—to set up another department to oversee Thriving Kids.

Ms Glanville : I'll just reiterate, in a slightly different way, what Mr Eaton has said. We look at them in a way which identifies the most egregious harms first and we move from there. Senator McAllister: Senator, the code of conduct is published, then the legislation that establishes this organisation, the regulator, sets out what the penalties can be if a person breaches the code of conduct when they're supplying a service as part of the NDIS. Senator McAllister: I don't want to stretch the tolerance, Senator Hanson, but the legislation before the parliament increases the penalties that can be levied by the commission or by a court in some instances up to 40 times, particularly where the safety of a person has been put at risk.

Senator HANSON: I can appreciate that it gets to court and it stalls in the courts. But isn't that being reactive? What I'm asking is: who actually gives the unregistered providers the code of conduct?

Senator HANSON: It's an article that they read—is that right?

Ms Glanville : No.

Senator HANSON: How do they do it?

Ms Glanville : It's a set of requirements that they have to adhere to.

These are people who were either not on income support, so previously were not eligible, or had less than eight hours work capacity. We refer to it as meaningful engagement, and it's really putting back the relationship between a provider and a participant and creating that joint plan and tailored approach towards achieving a meaningful job outcome for participants. Since we started in November, the vast majority—it's around 90 per cent of the plans—are using that meaningful engagement job plan to support it.
